lessons.title: How the atmosphere formed and changed
lessons.summary: Find out what the air is made of today, how volcanoes gave the early Earth a very different atmosphere, and how oceans, algae and plants transformed it over billions of years.
objectives: I can state the approximate proportions of the gases in today's atmosphere.
I can describe one theory of how the early atmosphere formed from volcanic activity.
I can explain how oxygen levels rose because of photosynthesis by algae and plants.
I can explain how carbon dioxide levels fell through dissolving in oceans, forming sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
I can evaluate why evidence about the early atmosphere is limited.

activities.title: The air today
activities.content:
## What you are breathing

The atmosphere has been roughly the same for the last **200 million years**. Its composition is:

| Gas | Approximate proportion |
|---|---|
| nitrogen, N₂ | about **78%** (roughly four-fifths) |
| oxygen, O₂ | about **21%** (roughly one-fifth) |
| argon, Ar | just under 1% |
| carbon dioxide, CO₂ | about **0.04%** |
| water vapour | variable, usually 0–4% |

The useful rough version for exams: **four-fifths nitrogen, one-fifth oxygen**, plus small amounts of other gases including the noble gases and carbon dioxide.

Notice how tiny the amount of carbon dioxide is. It is measured in **parts per million** (about 420 ppm), yet it has a huge effect on the climate, as you will see in the next lesson.

### A very different past

The Earth is about **4.6 billion years old**. For most of that time the atmosphere was nothing like today's. Working out what it was like is difficult because nobody was there to measure it, so scientists build **theories** from indirect evidence: the composition of gases from modern volcanoes, the chemistry of ancient rocks, and what we know about other planets.

Because the evidence is limited, these theories are still being refined. In exams you will usually be asked about **one** theory, the volcanic theory, and to recognise why it cannot be proved completely.

question.text: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere today is nitrogen?
question.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, roughly four-fifths.

activities.title: The early atmosphere: volcanoes
activities.content:
## The first billion years

One widely accepted theory says that during the first billion years of Earth's history there was **intense volcanic activity**. Volcanoes released huge quantities of gas, and these gases formed the early atmosphere.

### What the volcanoes released

- Mostly **carbon dioxide**, so the early atmosphere was largely CO₂ with little or no oxygen. This is thought to be similar to the atmospheres of **Mars and Venus** today, which are dominated by carbon dioxide.
- **Water vapour**, which condensed as the Earth cooled to form the **oceans**.
- Smaller amounts of **nitrogen**, **methane** and **ammonia**.

### Why no oxygen?

Volcanoes do not give out oxygen. Any free oxygen would in any case have reacted quickly with the other gases and with iron in the rocks. So for the first two billion years or so there was almost **no oxygen** in the air, and no animals could have survived.

### Why is nitrogen so abundant today?

Nitrogen was released by volcanoes in small amounts, but it is a very **unreactive** gas. Over billions of years it simply **built up** because very little of it was removed, while the more reactive gases were used up by other processes. That is how a minor volcanic gas came to make up four-fifths of the air.

activities.title: Worked example: comparing planets
activities.content:
**The table shows the atmospheres of three planets. What does this suggest about the early Earth?**

| Gas | Venus | Mars | Earth today |
|---|---|---|---|
| carbon dioxide | 96% | 95% | 0.04% |
| nitrogen | 3.5% | 2.7% | 78% |
| oxygen | trace | 0.1% | 21% |

**Reasoning**

1. Venus and Mars both have atmospheres that are **mostly carbon dioxide** with almost no oxygen. They formed at the same time as Earth from similar material, so it is reasonable to think the **early Earth was similar**.
2. Earth is now completely different. Something must have **removed** almost all the carbon dioxide and **added** a lot of oxygen. Venus and Mars have no oceans and no life, and those are exactly the two things responsible on Earth.

**This is evidence, not proof.** It supports the volcanic theory, but other explanations are possible. Scientists say a theory is well supported when several independent lines of evidence point the same way.

**What an exam answer needs:** name the similarity (mostly CO₂, little oxygen), then state what it implies (early Earth probably the same).

question.text: According to the volcanic theory, which of the following describe the Earth's early atmosphere? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what volcanoes release and which gas is missing.
question.explanation: The early atmosphere was mostly carbon dioxide with water vapour and small amounts of nitrogen, methane and ammonia. There was little or no oxygen, so it was not like today's air.

options.feedback: Nitrogen was a minor gas that built up gradually over time.

activities.title: Oceans and the loss of carbon dioxide
activities.content:
## Where all the carbon dioxide went

The early atmosphere may have contained hundreds of times more carbon dioxide than today. Three processes locked most of it away.

### 1. Dissolving in the oceans

As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. **Carbon dioxide dissolves in water.** Enormous amounts of CO₂ dissolved into the new oceans, removing it from the air.

### 2. Forming sedimentary rocks

In the oceans, dissolved carbon dioxide reacted with minerals to form **carbonates**, which precipitated out. Sea creatures also used carbonates to build shells and skeletons. When they died, these sank and were compressed over millions of years into **sedimentary rocks** such as **limestone** (calcium carbonate). The carbon is now trapped in rock.

### 3. Forming fossil fuels

Plants and algae took in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and built it into their bodies. When they died and were buried without oxygen, they were slowly turned into **coal**. Tiny sea organisms became **crude oil and natural gas**. All of this carbon came originally from atmospheric CO₂.

### A carbon store

Limestone, coal, oil and gas are all **carbon stores**. Together they explain how carbon dioxide dropped from most of the atmosphere to just 0.04%. When we burn fossil fuels or heat limestone to make cement, we release some of that ancient carbon back into the air.

question.text: Match each process to the way it reduced carbon dioxide in the early atmosphere.
question.hint: Think about water, rocks and buried plants.
question.explanation: CO₂ dissolved in the newly formed oceans; carbonates from sea creatures and minerals became limestone; buried plants and sea organisms became fossil fuels.

pairs.right: carbon dioxide dissolved in the water

pairs.left: burial of dead plants and organisms
pairs.right: carbon locked into coal, oil and gas

activities.title: The rise of oxygen
activities.content:
## Life changes the air

About **2.7 billion years ago**, simple organisms called **algae** evolved in the oceans. They could carry out **photosynthesis**, using sunlight to make food from carbon dioxide and water:

**carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

This reaction does two things at once: it **removes carbon dioxide** from the air and **releases oxygen** into it.

### A slow build-up

At first the oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the oceans, forming iron oxides that settled as rock. Only once that iron was used up did oxygen begin to collect in the atmosphere.

Over the next **billion years or so**, algae and then **plants** spread across the oceans and later the land, and oxygen levels gradually climbed towards today's 21%.

### Why it mattered

- Once there was enough oxygen, **animals** could evolve, because they need oxygen for respiration.
- Some of the oxygen high in the atmosphere formed the **ozone layer**, which blocks harmful ultraviolet light and made it safe for life to move onto land.

The timeline runs: volcanoes → oceans → algae → oxygen → animals. Every stage depends on the one before.

activities.title: Worked example: explaining a graph
activities.content:
**A graph shows oxygen in the atmosphere at close to 0% until about 2.4 billion years ago, then rising in steps to 21% by around 400 million years ago. Explain the shape.**

**Flat at zero for the first two billion years.** No organisms capable of photosynthesis existed yet, and volcanoes release no oxygen. Any oxygen that did form reacted with iron and other substances.

**The first rise, about 2.4 billion years ago.** Algae had evolved and been photosynthesising for some time. Once the dissolved iron in the oceans had been used up, oxygen could start to accumulate in the air.

**Continued rise over the next two billion years.** Photosynthesising organisms became more numerous and spread; land plants appeared around 470 million years ago and added to the total.

**Levelling off at 21%.** Oxygen production by photosynthesis came into balance with oxygen use by respiration, decay and combustion, so the level has stayed roughly constant.

In a question like this, link each **change on the graph** to a **process** and say what caused it. Dates are helpful but the reasoning earns the marks.

question.text: Put these events in the order in which they happened in the history of the Earth's atmosphere.
question.hint: Start with the volcanoes. Oxygen needs living things to make it.
question.explanation: Volcanoes released gases, water vapour condensed into oceans, CO₂ dissolved and formed carbonates, algae evolved and began photosynthesis, oxygen built up, and eventually animals could evolve.
order: Volcanoes release carbon dioxide and water vapour
Water vapour condenses to form the oceans
Carbon dioxide dissolves in the oceans and forms carbonate rocks
Oxygen builds up in the atmosphere

question.text: A sample of air has a volume of 500 cm³. Using the approximate composition of the atmosphere (21% oxygen), calculate the volume of oxygen in the sample in cm³.

Scientists believe the Earth's early atmosphere was very different from the atmosphere today.

(a) Describe how the early atmosphere is thought to have formed and state its main gas.

(b) Explain two ways in which the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decreased.

(c) Explain how the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere increased.

(d) Suggest why scientists cannot be certain about the composition of the early atmosphere.
question.hint: Volcanoes; oceans, rocks and photosynthesis; algae; and the lack of direct evidence from billions of years ago.
question.explanation: (a) Intense volcanic activity released gases; the main gas was carbon dioxide. (b) Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans; it formed carbonates that became sedimentary rocks such as limestone; it was taken in by photosynthesis and locked into fossil fuels. (c) Algae and later plants carried out photosynthesis, which releases oxygen. (d) It happened billions of years ago, so there is no direct evidence; scientists rely on indirect evidence and theories.

markScheme.criterion: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans
Formed carbonates / sedimentary rocks / limestone, or locked into fossil fuels by photosynthesis
Algae (and plants) evolved and carried out photosynthesis, releasing oxygen
No direct evidence because it was billions of years ago / no one was there to measure it / evidence is limited

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Today's air: about **78% nitrogen**, **21% oxygen**, under 1% argon, **0.04% carbon dioxide**, variable water vapour. Stable for 200 million years.
- **Volcanic theory**: intense volcanic activity in the first billion years gave an atmosphere of mostly **carbon dioxide** with water vapour and small amounts of nitrogen, methane and ammonia, and **little or no oxygen**, similar to Mars and Venus today.
- Water vapour condensed to form the **oceans**.
- CO₂ decreased because it **dissolved in the oceans**, formed **carbonates and sedimentary rocks** (limestone), and was locked into **fossil fuels**.
- **Nitrogen built up** because it is unreactive.
- **Algae** (2.7 billion years ago) and later **plants** carried out **photosynthesis**, releasing oxygen; once it built up, **animals** could evolve.
- Evidence is **limited** because it all happened billions of years ago, so the early atmosphere theories cannot be proved conclusively.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these are carbon stores that formed from carbon dioxide in the early atmosphere? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Limestone (a sedimentary carbonate rock) and coal (a fossil fuel) both contain carbon that came originally from atmospheric CO₂. Granite is an igneous rock and does not contain carbonates; argon is a noble gas.

practiceQuestions.text: The current carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere is about 420 parts per million. Express this as a percentage of the atmosphere. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
practiceQuestions.hint: Parts per million ÷ 10 000 gives a percentage.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how the evolution of algae led to an increase in oxygen in the atmosphere and eventually allowed animals to evolve.
practiceQuestions.hint: Name the process, say what it produces, and say why animals need it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Algae carried out photosynthesis, which uses carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen. Over hundreds of millions of years the oxygen built up in the atmosphere. Animals need oxygen for respiration, so they could evolve only once there was enough.

markScheme.criterion: Which released oxygen that built up in the atmosphere over a long time
Animals need oxygen for respiration so could evolve once oxygen levels were high enough

practiceQuestions.text:
The atmospheres of Mars and Venus are about 95% carbon dioxide with almost no oxygen.

(a) Explain how this evidence supports the theory that the Earth's early atmosphere was mostly carbon dioxide.

(b) Explain why the Earth's atmosphere is now so different from those of Mars and Venus.

(c) Explain why this evidence supports the theory but does not prove it.
practiceQuestions.hint: The planets formed together. Earth has oceans and life. Evidence from other planets is indirect.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The planets formed at the same time from similar material, so Earth's early atmosphere was probably similar to theirs: mostly carbon dioxide with little oxygen. (b) On Earth, oceans formed and carbon dioxide dissolved in them and formed carbonate rocks, and living organisms carried out photosynthesis which removed CO₂ and added oxygen; Mars and Venus have no oceans or life. (c) It is indirect evidence; the early Earth could have been different, and there is no direct evidence from that time, so the theory cannot be confirmed with certainty.

markScheme.criterion: Planets formed at the same time / from the same material so Earth was probably similar (mostly CO₂)
On Earth carbon dioxide dissolved in oceans / formed carbonate rocks
Photosynthesis by algae/plants removed CO₂ and added oxygen; Mars and Venus have no life/oceans
The evidence is indirect / there is no direct evidence from billions of years ago so the theory cannot be proved

practiceQuestions.text: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere today is oxygen?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Oxygen makes up about 21% of the atmosphere, roughly one-fifth. Nitrogen makes up most of the rest.

practiceQuestions.hint: Volcanoes released the early gases. Think about which gases were present in large amounts and which were almost absent.

It contained very little oxygen, and nitrogen was only a minor gas that built up gradually, so it was not richer in nitrogen than today's air.

It contained large amounts of water vapour that later condensed.
It contained a higher proportion of nitrogen than today.

practiceQuestions.text: Carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere in several ways. Match each process to the carbon store it produced.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about sea water, rock and buried living things.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolved directly into the oceans; dissolved carbonates were precipitated and built into shells that became sedimentary rocks such as limestone; carbon taken in by photosynthesis was buried with dead organisms and became fossil fuels.

pairs.left: carbon dioxide dissolved directly into sea water
carbonates precipitated and shells of sea creatures were compressed
dead plants and organisms were buried and compressed
pairs.right: fossil fuels such as coal and oil

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events in order to show how carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere ended up as limestone.
practiceQuestions.hint: The gas must be released before it can dissolve, and it must dissolve before sea creatures can use it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Volcanoes released carbon dioxide; the Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to form oceans; carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans; sea creatures used the dissolved carbonates to build shells; the shells and sediment were compressed over millions of years into limestone.
order: Intense volcanic activity releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
The Earth cools and water vapour condenses to form the oceans
Carbon dioxide dissolves in the ocean water
Sea creatures use dissolved carbonates to build their shells
Shells and sediments are compressed into limestone

practiceQuestions.text: A gas syringe contains 250 cm³ of air. Using the approximate composition of the atmosphere (78% nitrogen), calculate the volume of nitrogen in the syringe in cm³.

The composition of the Earth's atmosphere has been roughly the same for the last 200 million years.

(a) Describe the composition of the atmosphere today. Give the approximate percentages of the two main gases.

(b) Explain why nitrogen gradually became the most abundant gas in the atmosphere.

(c) Explain how the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere increased.

(d) Describe how carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere became locked up in sedimentary rocks.
practiceQuestions.hint: Four-fifths and one-fifth. Nitrogen does not react easily. Oxygen comes from living things. Think about the oceans, shells and layers of sediment.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) About 78% (four-fifths) nitrogen and about 21% (one-fifth) oxygen, with small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases such as argon. (b) Nitrogen was released by volcanoes (and by reactions such as ammonia with oxygen); because it is very unreactive it was not removed, so it built up over time. (c) Algae and later plants carried out photosynthesis, which releases oxygen. (d) Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans; it formed insoluble carbonates, which precipitated and were built into the shells of sea creatures; these were deposited as sediment and compressed into rocks such as limestone.

markScheme.criterion: Nitrogen is unreactive so it was not removed and built up over time (released by volcanoes)
Photosynthesis by algae and plants released oxygen
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans
Formed carbonates / shells, deposited as sediment and compressed into limestone
